The other triggers ('feeling physically unwell', 'unpredictable situations') and the negative appraisals describe generalized vulnerability and loss of control, but 'similar cars' introduces a highly specific cue that does not cohere with the rest of the formulation or trauma type.

Here there are no Memory or Threat items providing that connection, making this trigger clinically incoherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

With Threat node absent and no trigger content clearly tied to vigilance for danger, this appraisal is weakly matched to the trigger pattern and stands out as formulation-incongruent in this profile.

vignette:
Minh remembers the sky turning orange. He was forty-eight then, a policy analyst specializing in environmental risk assessment—he had read the projections, attended the briefings, filed the reports. None of that prepared him for the moment he had to choose: take the main road, which was already clogged with cars, or the winding canyon road he knew less well. He chose the canyon road. Within minutes, the smoke was so thick he could not see the hood of his car. The heat rattled the windows. He abandoned the vehicle and ran on foot, eventually lying flat in a culvert as the firestorm passed overhead. He survived physically unharmed, but something essential had broken in his sense of himself.

Now fifty-one, Minh has spent the three years since that night trying to make sense of what happened. He goes over it again and again: the hesitation, the faulty judgment, the surge of pure panic that overrode his training. He had always thought of himself as calm, rational, the person others relied on. Now he is certain he cannot rely on himself. This conviction deepens every time he feels a threat approaching. A low-grade fever or the congestion of a common cold reliably sends him into a state of high alert; the physical sensation of being unwell reminds him viscerally of the suffocating helplessness he felt in the culvert. His heart races, his palms sweat, and he thinks: I am falling apart. My reactions since the fire mean that I am going crazy. He has said this out loud exactly once, to his wife Kim, and her expression of worry only confirmed his fear.

Minh has developed a quiet but relentless hypervigilance. He checks the weather forecast hourly. He monitors the air quality index on his phone the way other people check their email. He has to be especially careful, he tells himself, because you never know what can happen next. This attitude has seeped into every corner of his life. At work, he has gradually withdrawn from his core responsibilities. The unpredictability of climate models, which he once found intellectually stimulating, now feels menacing and personal. He avoids opening the wildfire risk spreadsheets. He requested a transfer to the budget analysis division, citing a desire for something more stable. His supervisor granted the request but noted the change in his performance. Minh knows his career has stalled—he has been passed over twice for the senior analyst position he once expected—and he tells himself it is better than the alternative: being exposed, daily, to data that feels like an accusation.

At home, his need for order has created a quiet tension. He keeps a go-bag in the trunk of his car, though he never unpacked the one he grabbed that night. He has mapped three evacuation routes from his house and refuses to take guests into areas without clear road signage. Kim has grown tired of his rigidity. She wanted to plan a weekend trip to a forest cabin, and Minh could not bring himself to explain why the very idea of it—the isolation, the unpredictable terrain, the risk of smoke from a distant fire—filled him with dread. He said no without giving a real reason. She accused him of being distant. He did not correct her.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a minor event at the age of fifty-one. A neighbor held an early evening barbecue, and the wind carried the smell of burning charcoal across the yard. Minh was inside reading. His throat closed. He dropped to the floor without deciding to, his hands over his head. When he came back to himself, nearly half an hour had passed. He had scratched his own forearm without noticing. That evening, he told Kim he thought he was losing his mind, and this time she did not argue. She found him a therapist. Minh came to the first session with his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He is afraid of what he might do the next time he smells smoke or feels his heart race for no reason. He is afraid his wife will see him unravel. But underneath all of that, what he wants most is to believe—just once—that the man who made the wrong turn is not the only version of himself he has left.
